text: Careful initialisation gives a network a good start, but training immediately begins to change the weights, and as early layers change, the numbers they pass forward drift in size and position. Each later layer is then learning against a moving target. Normalisation is a simple, almost blunt remedy: at certain points in the network, rescale the numbers so that they always arrive in a standard range.

The operation is the one a teacher uses when grading on a curve. Take a group of numbers, subtract their mean so they are centred on zero, and divide by their standard deviation so their typical size is one, adding a tiny constant first so that we never divide by zero. Then, because the network may genuinely need a different centre or scale, it multiplies by a learned scale and adds a learned shift, called gamma and beta, so normalisation never removes anything the network cannot put back.

The question is which group of numbers to normalise together. Batch normalisation, introduced by Ioffe and Szegedy in 2015, takes one feature at a time and computes its mean and spread across all the examples in the current batch. It made deep image networks far easier to train, but it ties each example to its neighbours in the batch, so it needs running averages at test time and struggles when batches are small.

Layer normalisation, from Ba, Kiros and Hinton in 2016, turns the grid the other way. It takes one example at a time and normalises across that example's own features, so each example, or in a language model each token, is normalised entirely on its own. Nothing depends on the batch, and training and inference behave identically, which is exactly what sequence models need.

Why does this help so much? The original explanation, that it stops each layer's inputs from shifting, is still debated, and later work suggests a bigger effect is a smoother loss landscape that is easier to descend. What is not in doubt is the practical result: normalised networks tolerate larger learning rates, and they train faster and more reliably.

Every transformer block in a language model contains layer normalisation. GPT-2 places it at the entrance to each sub-block rather than after it, which makes very deep stacks more stable, and many recent models, such as LLaMA, use a simpler cousin called RMSNorm, which skips subtracting the mean and only divides by the root mean square.

So normalisation recentres and rescales the numbers flowing through a network, across the batch for images and within each token for language. Next we turn from making training work to making it generalise, with a surprisingly strange idea called dropout.
